Week 8: Capacity and consent

Apply the Health Care Consent Act (HCCA): when consent is needed, how to judge capacity, what makes consent valid, and who decides when the patient can't.

The case: Doris, 83
  • Alzheimer's disease. Her daughter Maria, a high school principal, comes to visits.
  • Clinic: pain since a fall. Ibuprofen was increased and Tylenol #3 added. Bloodwork shows type 2 diabetes, so you prescribe metformin, suggest stopping Tylenol #3 and offer physio. Maria says Doris dislikes appointments and Maria has little time to drive her.
  • Hospital: floridly delirious, with fluctuating cognition. Wants to go home and refuses treatment. The team thinks she may need the ICU for urgent dialysis.
  • The EMR lists her other daughter, Lisa, as Power of Attorney for Personal Care. No other documentation exists.
  • Doris has told everyone she would not want ICU care or dialysis in hospital.
When consent applies (s.2) Assigned reading
  • Treatment is anything done for a therapeutic, preventive, palliative, diagnostic, cosmetic or other health-related purpose. It includes a plan of treatment.
  • Not treatment: assessing capacity, taking a history, examining, sharing an assessment or diagnosis, hospital admission, personal assistance, and treatment that poses little or no risk.
  • In the case: bloodwork, metformin, stopping Tylenol #3, physio, and ICU with dialysis each need consent.
Capacity (s.4 and s.15) Assigned reading
  • Two parts. The person can understand the information relevant to the decision, and appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding or not deciding.
  • Presume capacity unless you have reasonable grounds to think otherwise.
  • Capacity is specific to each treatment and can change over time. Delirium fluctuates, so reassess.
When family does the talking
  • Seek consent from a capable patient before involving family.
  • Keep the patient's wishes as the priority while you work with family. Protect confidentiality and autonomy.
  • Include the patient and family in the care team, with shared decision-making where it fits.
Valid consent (s.11) Assigned reading
  • Four elements: it relates to the treatment, it is informed, it is voluntary, and it is not obtained through misrepresentation or fraud.
  • Informed means the patient gets the nature of the treatment, expected benefits, material risks, material side effects, alternatives, and the likely consequences of no treatment, and gets answers to their questions.
  • Consent can be express or implied.
Substitute decision-makers (s.20) Assigned reading
  1. Guardian of the person
  2. Attorney for personal care (POA)
  3. Representative appointed by the Consent and Capacity Board (CCB)
  4. Spouse or partner
  5. Child or parent
  6. Parent with right of access only
  7. Brother or sister
  8. Any other relative
  • The SDM must be capable, at least 16 (unless they are the patient's parent), available and willing, and not barred by a court order.
  • The Public Guardian and Trustee decides when no one qualifies, or when equal-ranked SDMs disagree.
How the SDM decides (s.21) Assigned reading
  1. Follow a prior capable wish that applies to the situation, expressed when the patient was 16 or older.
  2. If there is none, or it can't be followed, decide in the patient's best interests: their values and beliefs, current wishes, and whether the benefit outweighs the risk.
  • Prior wishes come before best interests. In the case, Doris's wish against ICU care and dialysis guides her SDM.
  • If an SDM ignores a prior wish, the health practitioner can apply to the CCB.
Emergencies (s.25) Assigned reading
  • You may treat without consent when a delay would prolong severe suffering or risk serious bodily harm.
  • Not if you know the person refused that treatment while capable.
POA documentation Outside the module
  • A power of attorney for personal care must be in writing, signed and witnessed. An EMR entry alone is not proof, so ask to see the document.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

Understanding the relevant information, and appreciating the reasonably foreseeable consequences of the decision.

Prior capable wishes that apply to the situation. Best interests only when there are none.

The Public Guardian and Trustee.

Week 9: Imposter syndrome

Explain imposter syndrome, see its relevance to your career, identify and reduce its effects, and know the supports.

What it is
  • Introduced by Clance and Imes in 1978. Many high-achieving women credited their success to luck, not their talents or qualifications.
  • About 70% of men and women feel it at some point.
  • A form of inaccurate self-assessment, linked to perfectionism.
  • Common in medicine because of its high-stakes, evaluative culture.
  • Triggers: poor performance or errors, with guilt, anxiety and self-doubt.
  • The profession does a poor job of preparing physicians to manage errors or seek support.
Consequences
  • Psychological wellbeing
  • Burnout
  • Clinical performance
  • Career advancement
  • Effectiveness as a teacher
  • Support for learners and peers
The case: Samantha

Evidence of imposter syndrome

  • Felt relieved and lucky to pass her first exam.
  • Spent winter break exhausted, worrying about how she did.
  • Afraid her peers would find out she wasn't good enough.
  • Grew more reserved and pulled away from peers.
  • Anxious about every assignment and quiz, formative or not.

Risk factors

  • Rejected on her first application with no interviews, and no Master's spot.
  • Worked as a data entry clerk and banquet server before getting in.
  • Hard transition back to school.
  • Older than her peers, from a smaller university outside Ontario.
  • Felt she couldn't fit in, and compared herself to peers who answered easily.
The imposter cycle Outside the module
  1. Task
  2. Anxiety
  3. Over-prepare or procrastinate
  4. Success
  5. Credit goes to luck or effort
  6. Praise discounted
  7. Fraud feeling grows, repeat
Helping a peer Outside the module

Signs

Goes quiet in small group, skips social events, puts themselves down, deflects compliments, gets anxious over low-stakes tasks.

  1. Check in privately and casually.
  2. Listen first. Don't rush to fix it.
  3. Normalize it by sharing your own self-doubt.
  4. Point to evidence of their competence.
  5. Point them to supports. Escalate to the Learner Experience Office (LEO) or faculty for signs of depression or safety concerns.
Supports
Students
Schulich Learner Experience Office personal counselling (listed in the module).
Physicians
CMA Physician Wellness Hub (listed in the module).

Outside the module Also: Western Wellness and mentors for students, the PARO 24/7 helpline for residents, and the OMA Physician Health Program for physicians.

In the session
  • Give a classmate a genuine, specific compliment, and notice how hard it is to accept one.
  • Share past experiences of imposter syndrome.
  • Privately write down 3 things you are great at.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

An inaccurate one, linked to perfectionism.

Poor performance or errors, with guilt, anxiety and self-doubt.

Any three of: worse psychological wellbeing, burnout, weaker clinical performance, slower career advancement, less effective teaching, less support for learners and peers.

Week 10: Implicit bias and SDH

Reduce the impact of implicit bias, use the social determinants of health (SDH) and financial supports to plan care, and lower barriers for underrepresented groups.

Why it matters
  • The privilege we experience is largely a function of luck. Many opportunities come from the context we were born into, not hard work.
  • Know your patient's context and meet them where they are, so the plan is one they can follow.
Implicit bias
  • Unconscious, and informed by all of your past experiences. Don't feel bad about having it. It can't be helped.
  • The space between the biased thought and your reaction is where you have a choice.
  • Mindfulness: focusing your awareness on the present moment while calmly acknowledging your feelings, thoughts and bodily sensations.
  • Sleep matters. Alkozei and colleagues showed sleep restriction increased implicit bias and influenced explicit decisions.
  • You are least likely to fall victim to bias when well rested, fed and hydrated.
  • The Harvard Implicit Association Test (IAT) helps identify your biases and guides what to explore next.
  • Under stress, practise self-compassion and remember most patients are doing what they think is reasonable.
The case: Andrea

Your state

Poor sleep, little breakfast, no lunch by 1:30 pm.

First impressions

Smells of cigarettes, staring at her phone, obese, poor hygiene. Has a family doctor but came to a walk-in for 1 month of low back pain.

What the history showed

  • Feels judged and dismissed by her family doctor, waits 3 to 4 months for 5-minute visits.
  • No reliable transportation, and the walk-in is closer to home.
  • Cut down to half a pack a day.
  • PSW in long-term care, working overtime after staffing cuts, came straight from a shift.
  • Single mom. Her son had a fever, so she was checking her phone.

The plan that failed

Heating pad, NSAIDs and a physio referral. She came back unimproved because she couldn't afford the NSAIDs or physio. She is on probation at work, worried about missing time, and has no health benefits yet.

Reducing bias Assigned reading

van Ryn's 3 strategies

Perspective-taking
Picture the visit from the patient's side, then check it with them.
Partnership-building
Use "we" and "let's", and name shared goals.
Protect cognitive resources
Sleep, eat, manage stress, and fix system pressures.

System 1 and System 2

  • System 1 is fast and automatic and steers most behaviour. System 2 is slow and deliberate.
  • Bias acts most under fatigue, stress, hunger, time pressure and heavy cognitive load.
Bias in care (CPSO examples) Assigned reading
  • Women are 3 times less likely to be referred for knee replacement when it is indicated.
  • Black and Hispanic patients get less pain medication despite higher pain scores.
  • COPD is underdiagnosed in women.
  • Patients sense bias, so trust, adherence and follow-up drop.
SDH and money
  • OHIP covers much of the immediate evaluation, but often less of the plan.
  • Income sources to know: employment, Ontario Works (OW), ODSP, CPP Disability (CPPD), CPP and Employment Insurance (EI). Some come with drug and health service coverage.
SDH and coverage details Outside the module
  • SDH are the social and economic conditions that shape health. In Andrea's case: income, employment and working conditions, caregiving, access to care, social support and smoking.
  • WSIB: work injuries. Covers wages, drugs and physio.
  • Ontario Drug Benefit: age 65 and over, under 25 without a private plan (OHIP+), OW or ODSP, long-term care, home care, Trillium.
  • Trillium: high drug costs relative to income, with an income-based deductible.
  • OHIP physio: age 19 and under, 65 and over, a hospital stay or day surgery in the last 12 months, or OW or ODSP.

Ontario government pages, checked Nov 4, 2026.

Changing the patient Outside the module

The module asks how your plan changes for each patient. Suggested answers:

Newcomer, limited English
Professional interpreter, not family. Plain language and teach-back.
Opioid use disorder
Avoid diagnostic overshadowing. Non-opioid care first. Check the Narcotics Monitoring System.
Schizophrenia or bipolar
Avoid diagnostic overshadowing. NSAIDs raise lithium levels. Ask about ODSP.
Age 75 with mild cognitive impairment
Presume capacity and speak to her directly. Avoid oral NSAIDs. Screen for falls.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

In the space between the biased thought and your reaction.

It increased implicit bias and influenced explicit decisions.

She couldn't afford NSAIDs or physio, had no benefits yet, and was on probation at work.

Week 12: Environment and health

Describe how environmental and climate concerns contribute to or trigger illness, identify vulnerable patient groups, and prescribe healthy choices that help both patient and local environment.

The case: Sarah, 21
  • University student in the ER with right groin swelling, fatigue and a temperature of 39°C.
  • Unwell for a week. The lump grew from grape-sized to multiple small strawberry-sized masses. Fevers on and off for 3 days.
  • Mild headaches, myalgias and arthralgias. Lower appetite.
  • Summer in a chemistry lab and playing ultimate frisbee. Camped at Pinery Provincial Park 2 weeks ago.
  • Father had colon cancer in his early 50s. Mother has hypertension and lupus.
  • Exam: BP 96/60, HR 115, T 38.6°C. Possible mild splenomegaly. Multiple tender, soft, rubbery right groin nodes of 1 to 2 cm, not very mobile. A 5 to 6 cm red, circular rash on the back of her upper leg.
  • No neck or armpit nodes.
Reading the case Outside the module
  • Lyme disease fits best. A large circular rash after camping, with fever, is erythema migrans.
  • Climate link: Pinery is a tick area, and warmer temperatures expand tick range.
  • Disease of public health significance: Lyme is one, so it must be reported to public health.
  • Differential: mono, cat scratch disease, STIs, lymphoma, local skin infection.
  • The lab solvents don't explain her illness.
What the module asks you to discuss
  • Temperature extremes and changes, and their effect on vector-borne infections.
  • Environmental and occupational exposure to UV light, certain herbicides and pesticides, and solvents.
  • Measures in primary care to improve a patient's climate resilience.
  • How your hospital or clinic can cut its environmental footprint.
  • How you can advocate for your patients' current and future health.
Readings
  • McCally: environment and health overview
  • Galanis and Ogden: climate change and emerging diseases
  • Chekuri and Harper: climate-smart health care and the family physician
  • Clapp: environment and cancer

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

Camping at Pinery 2 weeks earlier and a large circular rash, with fever, arthralgias and myalgias.

Temperature changes affecting vector-borne infections, and exposure to UV, herbicides, pesticides and solvents.

Week 13: People with disabilities

Give respectful, inclusive, patient-centred care by adapting communication, supporting autonomy and recognizing barriers to equitable care.

Core idea
  • Disability is not a tragedy, but a difference.
  • Gord, 42: cerebral palsy. Uses a custom communication board. Support worker Ryan.
  • Brandy: cri-du-chat syndrome. Came to the ED after a fall with a suspected head injury. Support worker Denise.
  • Disability, stigma and system barriers affect access to safe, equitable, patient-centred care.
Communication
  • Greet with respect, attend to comfort and the need for an interpreter, and orient the patient to the interview.
  • Use communication aids: communication boards and books, social stories, interpreters, American Sign Language.
  • Bring in health care navigators and patient advocates for other barriers.
  • Speak to the patient first. Include support workers, with the patient's permission.
  • Use appropriate nonverbal communication: positioning, posture, facial expression.
  • Use clear language, check for understanding, and clarify.
  • Build a shared plan with the patient, family and other professionals.
Agitation and challenging behaviour
  • It may reflect communication barriers, pain, fear, sensory overload, environmental stressors, unmet needs or underlying illness.
  • Many people with intellectual disabilities find it harder to regulate emotions or say what is wrong.
  • Long ED waits create extra challenges for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD).
Care for adults with developmental disabilities

Critical findings

  • Level of intellectual and adaptive functioning
  • Risk factors for abuse and neglect

Initial management

  • Assess ability to give voluntary, informed consent.
  • Get input and help from caregivers and support workers.
  • Start interdisciplinary care if needed.
  • Do screening and prevention, such as for infectious diseases and cancer.
  • Anticipate medium and long-term complications, such as psychosocial effects and safety.
Capacity
  • Patients are presumed capable.
  • Capacity is specific to each treatment decision.
Bias and anti-oppressive care
  • Reflect on your assumptions about people with disabilities, and how your values shape your communication.
  • Recognize the effects of stigma and discrimination on groups facing health inequities, including by race, ethnicity, immigration, income, religion, disability, gender identity, sexual orientation, weight and substance use.
  • Know your limits of competence.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

Any four of: communication barriers, pain, fear, sensory overload, environmental stressors, unmet needs, underlying illness.

The patient.

Decision-specific, and patients are presumed capable.

Week 14: Vaccination and public health

Counsel patients and families about vaccines and hesitancy, using patient-centred communication, informed consent, advocacy and public health principles.

The case: Sophie, 11
  • Due for HPV, a meningococcal booster and catch-up MMR. Vaccines were delayed by COVID-19, and the family moved from a rural area with poor access.
  • Her mother read online that vaccines cause infertility and developmental problems, thinks HPV is "too new" and that kids get "too many vaccines too early". A friend's child got fever and fatigue after vaccines.
  • Sophie is unsure, scared of needles and worried about side effects. Friends told her "these diseases do not exist anymore".
  • Part 2: a measles exposure at school, with possible exclusion for under-vaccinated students. After catch-up shots, Sophie has mild fever, fatigue and a sore arm the next day.
Vaccine hesitancy Nicole's Notes
  • Delay in accepting, or refusing, vaccines despite available services.
  • Most hesitant parents under-immunize. 3% of parents refuse outright.

Causes named in the module

  • Safety concerns
  • Misinformation on social media and online
  • Mistrust of institutions
  • Prior negative health care experiences
  • Cultural beliefs
  • Trouble accessing care

Approach

  • Prepare before the visit and set aside extra time.
  • Use presumptive and motivational interviewing techniques to find the specific concern.
  • Use simple, clear language for disease risks and vaccine benefits and risks.
  • Address pain head on.
  • Don't dismiss vaccine refusers from your practice.
  • Herd immunity does not guarantee personal protection.
What the module expects you to do
  • Assess immunization status and recommend a schedule, including catch-up.
  • Get an immunization history, including precautions and contraindications.
  • Explain how vaccines work and obtain informed consent.
  • Tell patients and families about possible reactions.
  • Counsel those who refuse.
  • Find patients who would benefit but don't come for routine visits.
  • Report and manage adverse reactions.
Adverse events (AEFI) Nicole's Notes
  • An unwanted or unexpected health effect within 6 weeks of immunization. It may or may not be caused by the vaccine.
  • Causes: a vaccine component (allergy), a defective product, the vaccination process (error or anxiety, such as syncope), or something unrelated.
  • Frequency scale: very common 10% or more, common 1 to 10%, uncommon 0.1 to 1%, rare 1 to 10 per 10,000, very rare under 1 per 10,000.
  • MMR: febrile seizures 3 to 9 per 10,000, thrombocytopenia 2 to 3 per 100,000, anaphylaxis 3 to 10 per million.
  • HPV and meningococcal ACYW: no adverse events listed.

Reporting

  • Mandatory for providers who give vaccines, under s.38 of the Health Protection and Promotion Act.
  • Fill out the AEFI form and send it to the local public health unit.
  • Local review, then provincial, then national (PHAC), then WHO. Manufacturers report serious events to Health Canada.
  • The Vaccine Injury Support Program supports people with serious, permanent injury from a vaccine.
Measles exposure Nicole's Notes
  • Vaccine within 72 hours for immunocompetent contacts over 6 months.
  • Immune globulin within 4 to 6 days for immunocompromised contacts, pregnant women and infants.
  • Measles needs airborne precautions in a negative pressure room.
  • Reportable diseases place legal obligations on clinicians.
Who regulates vaccines Nicole's Notes
  • Health Canada reviews and approves vaccines that are safe, work, meet manufacturing standards and have benefits that outweigh risks.
  • Trials run in phases: I (tens of volunteers), II (hundreds), III (tens of thousands).
  • Governments coordinate purchase and distribution. Monitoring continues after approval.
Outbreak steps Nicole's Notes
  1. Verify the outbreak
  2. Confirm the diagnosis
  3. Assemble the team
  4. Define and find cases
  5. Orient the data by person, place and time
  6. Generate hypotheses
  7. Test hypotheses
  8. Implement prevention and control
  9. Communicate the findings
  10. Debrief the team
Ontario funding and school rules Outside the module
  • Routine vaccines are publicly funded through Ontario's immunization schedule.
  • Public health units run Grade 7 school clinics for HPV, meningococcal and hepatitis B.
  • School attendance requires certain vaccines, with medical or conscience exemptions. Exempt students can be excluded during outbreaks.
  • Ontario has no fixed age of consent for treatment. A capable child can consent.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

Within 6 weeks of immunization.

MMR vaccine within 72 hours.

The local public health unit.
